items.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with eight weeks of symmetric pain and swelling in her metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with two hours of morning stiffness. Which investigation offers the highest specificity for rheumatoid arthritis?
items.exp: Anti-CCP antibodies exhibit high specificity (>95%) for rheumatoid arthritis and predict erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor has lower specificity and is positive in other connective tissue diseases and chronic infections.
r: Correct: Anti-CCP antibodies provide superior specificity (>95%) for rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but less specific, appearing in Sjogren syndrome, SLE and chronic infections.
ESR is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
ANA is sensitive for SLE but non-specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
items.kp: Anti-CCP has superior specificity over rheumatoid factor for rheumatoid arthritis.
items.source: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management

x.key: Anti-CCP antibodies offer highest specificity for rheumatoid arthritis.

others.D: ANA is not specific for RA.

x.pearl: Anti-CCP predicts radiological erosive progression in early rheumatoid arthritis.
x.clues: Symmetric MCP and PIP involvement with morning stiffness >60 minutes.
x.mech: Autoantibodies target citrullinated peptides generated by peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes in inflamed synovium.
x.lo: Identify the diagnostic serology of choice for rheumatoid arthritis.
x.rev: Anti-CCP is the most specific serological marker for rheumatoid arthritis.

next.text: Review rheumatoid arthritis diagnostic and management pathways.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with active rheumatoid arthritis. In accordance with national guidance, what is the recommended first-line disease-modifying strategy?
o: Conventional synthetic DMARD monotherapy (methotrexate) with short-course bridging corticosteroid
Infliximab monotherapy without prior conventional agents
Oral prednisolone monotherapy for twelve months
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone for six months
items.exp: NICE NG100 recommends first-line conventional synthetic DMARD monotherapy (oral methotrexate, leflunomide, or sulfasalazine) ideally within three months of symptom onset, with short-term bridging corticosteroid to control active synovitis while DMARDs take effect.
r: Correct: First-line strategy is csDMARD monotherapy with short-course bridging corticosteroid.
Biologic TNF inhibitors are second-line after failing two conventional DMARDs.
Steroid monotherapy causes osteoporosis and metabolic harm without disease modification.
NSAIDs provide symptomatic relief only and do not arrest erosive destruction.
items.kp: First-line rheumatoid therapy is csDMARD monotherapy plus short-course bridging steroid.
items.source: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management

x.key: csDMARD monotherapy with bridging corticosteroid is first-line.

others.B: Biologics are reserved for refractory disease.
others.C: Steroids alone do not modify long-term disease.
others.D: NSAIDs do not prevent joint erosions.

x.pearl: Start csDMARDs within three months of persistent symptom onset to preserve joint function.
x.mech: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and promotes adenosine release to downregulate synovial inflammation.
x.lo: State the first-line disease-modifying regimen for rheumatoid arthritis.
x.rev: NICE recommends csDMARD monotherapy with bridging corticosteroid.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is commenced on once-weekly oral methotrexate. Which co-prescription is standard to reduce mucosal and gastrointestinal adverse effects?
o: Folic acid taken on a different day of the week
Daily calcium carbonate with vitamin D
Ascorbic acid taken concurrently with methotrexate
items.exp: Co-prescribing folic acid (e.g., 5 mg once weekly on a day distinct from methotrexate) reduces methotrexate-induced nausea, abdominal cramps, oral ulcers and transaminitis without diminishing antirheumatic efficacy.
r: Correct: Folic acid reduces adverse effects and is taken on a different weekday.
Calcium and vitamin D prevent osteoporosis with corticosteroids, not methotrexate toxicity.
Ascorbic acid has no role in preventing methotrexate toxicity.
Aspirin can reduce methotrexate renal clearance and increase toxicity.
items.kp: Folic acid reduces methotrexate toxicity when taken on a separate day of the week.
items.source: British National Formulary: Methotrexate safety guidance

x.key: Folic acid co-prescription mitigates methotrexate toxicity.

others.B: Calcium is for bone protection with steroids.

x.pearl: Never prescribe daily methotrexate for inflammatory arthritis; dosing is strictly once weekly.
x.mech: Folic acid supplements folate pools depleted by methotrexate-mediated dihydrofolate reductase inhibition.
x.lo: Select the appropriate co-prescribed supplement for methotrexate therapy.
x.rev: Folic acid taken on a non-methotrexate day reduces mucosal and GI toxicity.

next.text: Review methotrexate prescribing and monitoring rules.

items.q: A 55-year-old man on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis presents with a four-week history of dry cough and progressive breathlessness on exertion. Oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. What is the most critical drug-related complication to suspect?
items.exp: Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic, potentially life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction characterised by dry cough, dyspnoea, fever and interstitial infiltrates. Methotrexate must be stopped immediately and urgent respiratory assessment arranged.
r: Correct: Methotrexate pneumonitis presents with dry cough, progressive dyspnoea and hypoxia.
Nephrotoxicity does not present with respiratory failure and cough.
Pericarditis is not a classic presentation of methotrexate lung toxicity.
Encephalopathy is seen with high-dose intravenous oncological methotrexate, not weekly low-dose oral therapy.
items.kp: New dry cough or dyspnoea on methotrexate suggests acute drug-induced pneumonitis.
items.source: British Society for Rheumatology DMARD safety guidelines

x.key: Methotrexate pneumonitis requires immediate drug cessation.
x.pearl: Any patient on methotrexate who develops a new dry cough or breathlessness requires urgent chest X-ray and drug cessation.
x.clues: Dry cough, progressive dyspnoea, hypoxia in a patient taking methotrexate.
x.ddx: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, pulmonary oedema.
x.mech: Type IV hypersensitivity and T-lymphocyte alveolitis driven by methotrexate exposure.
x.lo: Recognise methotrexate-induced pneumonitis and its immediate management.
x.rev: Stop methotrexate and evaluate urgently for acute interstitial pneumonitis.

items.q: Before initiating adalimumab in a patient with severe active rheumatoid arthritis refractory to methotrexate and leflunomide, which screening test is mandatory to prevent disease reactivation?
o: Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) and chest radiography for latent tuberculosis
items.exp: TNF-alpha is essential for granuloma maintenance. Anti-TNF agents like adalimumab risk life-threatening reactivation of latent tuberculosis; pre-treatment screening with IGRA (or Mantoux) and chest radiography is mandatory.
r: Correct: Screening for latent tuberculosis with IGRA and chest X-ray is mandatory before TNF inhibitors.
Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not indicated as pre-biologic screening.
Gastroscopy is not routinely required prior to TNF inhibitor initiation.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated without focal neurological signs.
items.kp: Screen all patients for latent tuberculosis prior to commencing TNF inhibitor therapy.
items.source: British Society for Rheumatology Biologic DMARD safety guidelines

x.key: Latent TB screening is mandatory prior to biologic TNF blockade.

others.C: Gastroscopy is not a screening requirement.

x.pearl: Disrupting TNF-alpha breaks down tuberculosis granulomas, leading to disseminated miliary infection.
x.clues: Severe active RA, preparing to start adalimumab.
x.ddx: Active tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis, atypical mycobacterial infection.
x.mech: TNF-alpha maintains macrophage aggregation and integrity within tuberculous caseating granulomas.
x.lo: State the mandatory infectious screening requirements prior to biologic therapy.
x.rev: IGRA and chest radiography must exclude latent tuberculosis before anti-TNF therapy.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for elective total hip replacement under general anaesthesia. Which preoperative investigation is critical to ensure anaesthetic airway safety?
o: Flexion and extension cervical spine radiographs to assess atlantoaxial subluxation
items.exp: Cervical spine involvement occurs in up to 30-50% of chronic rheumatoid arthritis patients, particularly atlantoaxial subluxation. Flexion and extension lateral radiographs assess the anterior atlantodental interval; unrecognised instability risks spinal cord transection during endotracheal intubation.
r: Correct: Cervical spine flexion and extension radiographs assess atlantoaxial stability before intubation.
Coronary CT is not routine without cardiac symptoms.
Echocardiography evaluates cardiac function but does not detect cervical spine instability.
Spirometry does not address the acute mechanical risk of spinal cord compression.
items.kp: Assess cervical spine flexion and extension in long-standing RA prior to general anaesthesia.
items.source: Association of Anaesthetists: Perioperative management of rheumatoid arthritis

x.key: Cervical flexion-extension films identify atlantoaxial subluxation.

others.B: Coronary CT is not an airway check.
others.C: Echo does not prevent cervical injury.

x.pearl: Transverse ligament erosion in RA allows the odontoid peg to compress the cervical cord during neck flexion.
x.clues: Long-standing erosive RA awaiting elective surgery under general anaesthesia.
x.ddx: Cervical myelopathy, central cord syndrome, traumatic subluxation.
x.mech: Pannus formation in the synovial joint around the dens erodes the transverse atlantal ligament.
x.lo: Identify the critical airway assessment in patients with chronic rheumatoid arthritis.
x.rev: Cervical flexion and extension X-rays detect atlantoaxial subluxation prior to intubation.

items.q: A 58-year-old man with severe nodular rheumatoid arthritis presents with recurrent leg ulcers, severe neutropenia (neutrophils 0.6 x 10^9/L) and palpable splenomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Felty syndrome is a rare manifestation of severe, long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly and neutropenia, predisposing to recurrent bacterial infections and skin ulceration.
r: Correct: Felty syndrome consists of rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia and splenomegaly.
Caplan syndrome is rheumatoid arthritis associated with pneumoconiosis and pulmonary nodules.
Adult-onset Still disease presents with high spiking fevers, salmon-pink rash and neutrophilia.
SLE causes cytopenias but is not the classic triad with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis.
items.kp: Felty syndrome is the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia and splenomegaly.
items.source: Oxford Textbook of Rheumatology: Extra-articular rheumatoid arthritis

x.key: Triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia defines Felty syndrome.

others.B: Caplan syndrome involves occupational lung nodules.
others.C: Still disease presents with fever and neutrophilia.
others.D: SLE features antinuclear antibodies and multiorgan involvement.

x.pearl: Patients with Felty syndrome face elevated risk of severe encapsulated bacterial infections.
x.clues: Nodular RA, leg ulcers, profound neutropenia, splenomegaly.
x.ddx: Large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, drug-induced agranulocytosis, lymphoma.
x.mech: Splenic sequestration and autoantibody-mediated peripheral destruction of mature neutrophils.
x.lo: Recognise the clinical triad defining Felty syndrome.
x.rev: Felty syndrome combines seropositive RA, splenomegaly and marked neutropenia.

next.text: Review systemic complications of rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate presents with a red, painful right eye with photophobia and deep boring ocular pain that wakes her from sleep. Visual acuity is normal, but the sclera shows violaceous injection that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Scleritis presents with severe, deep boring ocular pain waking the patient from sleep, radiating to the temple, and deep violaceous scleral injection that does not blanch with topical 2.5% phenylephrine (which blanches superficial episcleral vessels in episcleritis). Scleritis carries high risk of globe perforation and demands urgent ophthalmology referral.
r: Correct: Scleritis causes deep nocturnal boring pain and does not blanch with phenylephrine.
Episcleritis is mild or asymptomatic, causes pinkish injection and blanches completely with phenylephrine.
Conjunctivitis causes superficial discharge and grittiness without severe deep pain.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and flat bright red.
items.kp: Scleritis causes severe deep boring nocturnal pain and fails to blanch with topical phenylephrine.
items.source: Royal College of Ophthalmologists: Scleritis management guidelines

x.key: Deep boring pain failing to blanch with phenylephrine indicates scleritis.

others.B: Episcleritis blanches with phenylephrine and is mildly painful.

x.pearl: Scleritis strongly correlates with active systemic vasculitis and underlying connective tissue disease.
x.clues: Deep boring nocturnal pain, violaceous scleral injection resistant to phenylephrine blanching.
x.ddx: Episcleritis, acute anterior uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma.
x.mech: Immune complex deposition and necrotising granulomatous inflammation of the scleral collagen matrix.
x.lo: Differentiate scleritis from episcleritis in systemic inflammatory disease.
x.rev: Failure to blanch with phenylephrine confirms deep scleral inflammation in scleritis.

next.text: Review ocular manifestations of systemic autoimmune diseases.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis well-controlled on methotrexate and sulfasalazine announces she is planning pregnancy with her partner in four months. What is the most appropriate management regarding her DMARDs?
o: Stop methotrexate immediately and switch to pregnancy-compatible therapy such as certolizumab pegol
Continue methotrexate throughout pregnancy at reduced dose
Stop all medications and permit unmonitored disease flare
items.exp: Methotrexate is teratogenic and embryotoxic; BSR guidelines recommend stopping methotrexate at least three months prior to conception. Certolizumab pegol (a pegylated Fab fragment without an Fc domain) does not cross the placenta and is safe throughout pregnancy; sulfasalazine is also compatible with pregnancy when co-prescribed with 5 mg daily folic acid.
r: Correct: Methotrexate must be stopped at least three months prior to conception due to teratogenicity.
Methotrexate is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy.
Uncontrolled active RA increases adverse pregnancy outcomes; safe DMARDs must maintain control.
Leflunomide is highly teratogenic with prolonged enterohepatic circulation and is contraindicated.
items.kp: Stop methotrexate at least three months prior to conception; certolizumab pegol is pregnancy-safe.
items.source: British Society for Rheumatology prescribing in pregnancy and lactation guidelines

x.key: Methotrexate must be stopped before conception due to teratogenicity.

others.C: Active synovitis damages maternal and fetal health.

x.pearl: Certolizumab pegol lacks an active Fc region, preventing active transplacental transfer in all trimesters.
x.clues: Young female with RA planning pregnancy within four months.
x.ddx: Methotrexate embryopathy, miscarriage, intrauterine growth restriction.
x.mech: Methotrexate disrupts purine synthesis during fetal organogenesis, causing skeletal and neural defects.
x.lo: Manage DMARD therapy safely in patients planning pregnancy.
x.rev: Stop methotrexate 3 months pre-conception; switch to pregnancy-compatible agents.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis achieves minimal response to two conventional synthetic DMARDs. Her Disease Activity Score (DAS28) is calculated at 5.4. According to NICE criteria, what therapy is indicated next?
o: Biological DMARD therapy (such as a TNF inhibitor or rituximab) in combination with methotrexate
Increase oral corticosteroid dose indefinitely to 30 mg daily
Recommend surgical synovectomy for all affected joints
items.exp: NICE criteria permit biological DMARD initiation when rheumatoid arthritis has failed to respond to at least two conventional synthetic DMARDs (including methotrexate) and disease activity remains severe (DAS28 > 5.1 on two occasions one month apart).
r: Correct: Severe active disease (DAS28 > 5.1) failing two csDMARDs qualifies for biologic therapy.
Long-term high-dose steroid therapy causes unacceptable morbidity and is inappropriate.
NSAID monotherapy is ineffective for active erosive rheumatoid arthritis.
Surgical synovectomy is not indicated for widespread active polyarthritis.
items.kp: DAS28 greater than 5.1 after failing two conventional DMARDs qualifies for biologic therapy.

x.key: DAS28 > 5.1 after two csDMARDs meets criteria for biologic initiation.

others.B: High-dose steroid causes osteoporosis and infection.

x.pearl: DAS28 incorporates swollen joint count, tender joint count, ESR or CRP, and patient global assessment.
x.clues: Failure of two csDMARDs, DAS28 score 5.4.
x.mech: Biologics block specific inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6) or cellular targets (CD20 B-cells, T-cell costimulation).
x.lo: State the NICE eligibility threshold for biologic therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
x.rev: Failure of 2 csDMARDs with DAS28 > 5.1 qualifies for biologic therapy.
